work: Enarratio in Epistolam II B. Petri
source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. XIII (Montreuil)

1.title: ENARRATIO CAPITULI PRIMI : SIMON PETRUS, SERVUS ET APOSTOLUS JESU CHRISTI.
1.title_en: Exposition of the first chapter: Simon Peter, servant and apostle of Jesus Christ.

paras.t: Primitivam Ecclesiam impugnabant tyranni gladio materiali persecutionibusque diversis, hæretici autem doctrinis pestiferis. Quemadmodum ergo in prima epistola excellentissimus apostolici chori vertex, hortatus est fideles ad patientiam in adversis, ne persecutionibus cederent; ita in hac eos hortatur epistola, ne hæreticorum decipiantur figmentis. Scripsit autem beatissimus Petrus istam epistolam eis quibus et præcedentem. Nam infra ait: Hanc vobis, carissimi, secundam scribo epistolam.
paras.en: The tyrants assailed the primitive Church with the material sword and with persecutions of divers kinds, and the heretics with pestilent doctrines. As, then, in the first epistle the most excellent head of the apostolic choir exhorted the faithful to patience in adversity, that they might not yield to persecutions, so in this epistle he exhorts them not to be deceived by the inventions of heretics. Now the most blessed Peter wrote this epistle to the same people as the one before; for further on he says: [[2 Pet 3:1|this second epistle I write to you, my dearly beloved|Hanc vobis, carissimi, secundam scribo epistolam]].

paras.t: Itaque ait: Simon Petrus, servus servitute filialis, non servilis, timoris. Quemadmodum enim duplex est timor, ita duplex est servitus, puta servilis et filialis. De servo servitute servilis timoris fertur in Joanne: Servus non manet in domo in æternum; et alibi, Jam non dicam vos servos. Servo autem servitute filialis timoris dicitur apud Matthæum: Euge, serve bone et fidelis, intra in gaudium domini tui. Et apostolus Jesu Christi: quem Christus ascensurus ad Patrem, reliquit sui amoris et suæ auctoritatis vicarium, dans ei plenitudinem ecclesiasticæ potestatis super universalem Ecclesiam.
paras.en: So he says: [[1:1|Simon Peter, servant|Simon Petrus, servus]], by the servitude of filial, not servile, fear. For as fear is twofold, so servitude is twofold, namely servile and filial [servile fear dreads punishment; filial fear, that of a son, dreads offending one he loves]. Of the servant by the servitude of servile fear it is said in John: [[John 8:35|the servant abideth not in the house for ever|Servus non manet in domo in æternum]]; and elsewhere, [[John 15:15|I will not now call you servants|Jam non dicam vos servos]]. But to the servant by the servitude of filial fear it is said in Matthew: [[Matt 25:21|Well done, good and faithful servant|Euge, serve bone et fidelis]], [[Matt 25:21|Enter thou into the joy of thy lord|intra in gaudium domini tui]] [the margin gives Matt. xxv, 21 and 23, where the same words stand]. [[1:1|and apostle of Jesus Christ|Et apostolus Jesu Christi]]: whom Christ, when about to ascend to the Father, left as the vicar of his love and of his authority, giving him the fullness of ecclesiastical power over the universal Church.

paras.t: His qui eamdem nobiscum sortiti sunt fidem, id est, eamdem a Deo per infusionem acceperunt fidem, quam et nos a Deo suscepimus: quia, ut dicitur ad Ephesios, Unus Dominus, una fides, unum Baptisma. Dicitur autem fides una, unitate specifica, a suo objecto; sed ex parte subjectorum numeraliter multiplicatur. Denique princeps Apostolorum de se, et aliis ad fidem conversis, in generali jam loquitur. Nam ipsi gloriosi Apostoli habuerunt fidem perfectiorem, seu magis illuminatam, et ferventiore dilectione formatam ac firmiorem, quam ceteri Christiani: quia primitias Spiritus acceperunt, atque in omni virtute mirabiliter præfulgebant. Nihilo minus multi eorum quibus hæc scripsit, habuerunt fidem valde illuminatam, et æqualem in perfectione fidei plurimorum qui cum beatissimo erant Petro.
paras.en: [[1:1|to them that have obtained equal faith with us|His qui eamdem nobiscum sortiti sunt fidem]] [Denis's text reads *eamdem*, "the same" faith, where the Vulgate has *coæqualem*, "equal"; he takes up *coæqualem* below], that is, who have received from God by infusion the same faith that we too have received from God: because, as is said to the Ephesians, [[Eph 4:5|One Lord, one faith, one baptism.|Unus Dominus, una fides, unum Baptisma]] Now faith is called one by a unity of species, from its object; but on the side of its subjects it is multiplied in number [that is, what is believed is one and the same, but each believer has his own faith]. Further, the prince of the Apostles is now speaking in general, of himself and of the others converted to the faith. For the glorious Apostles themselves had a faith more perfect, that is, more enlightened, formed by a more fervent love, and firmer, than other Christians: because they received [[Rom 8:23|the firstfruits of the Spirit|primitias Spiritus]], and shone wonderfully in every virtue. None the less many of those to whom he wrote these things had a faith greatly enlightened, and equal in perfection to the faith of very many who were with the most blessed Peter.

paras.t: In justitia Dei et Salvatoris nostri Jesu Christi, id est cum justitia nobis per creationem a Deo salvatore infusa: quia non fidem dumtaxat, sed et alias quoque virtutes Deus infudit fidelibus. Et possunt ceteræ virtutes illæ infusæ, sub justitiæ appellatione intelligi, prout justitia est virtus communis: et omnis virtus, quædam justitia est, quia per eam habet se homo recte atque ut debet. Porro quod ait, Dei et Salvatoris nostri, quomodo referri possit ad eamdem increatam Personam, et quomodo ad distinctas Personas, dictum est in expositione præcedentis epistolæ.
paras.en: [[1:1|in the justice of our God and Saviour Jesus Christ|In justitia Dei et Salvatoris nostri Jesu Christi]], that is, with the justice infused into us by creation [that is, created in the soul by God, not acquired by our own acts] from God the Saviour: because God has infused into the faithful not faith alone, but the other virtues as well. And those other infused virtues can be understood under the name of justice, inasmuch as justice is a general virtue [Denis's word is *communis*: justice taken broadly, as the rightness of the whole man]: and every virtue is a kind of justice, because by it a man stands rightly and as he ought. Further, how the words [[1:1|our God and Saviour|Dei et Salvatoris nostri]] can be referred to the same uncreated Person, and how to distinct Persons, has been said in the exposition of the preceding epistle[[Jas 1:1||]] [the margin refers to the commentary on James 1:1, "the servant of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ"].

paras.t: Vel quod ait, In justitia Dei, exponendum est de increata justitia Dei, ut sit sensus: His qui coæqualem nobiscum sortiti sunt fidem in justitia Dei, ita quod justo Dei judicio fides illorum reputata est æqualis fidei nostræ. Sicque quod ait, In justitia, determinat quod dixerat, Coæqualem. Potest etiam determinare participium istud, Sortiti sunt: ita quod sit sensus, quod justo Dei judicio data est eis fides talis ac tanta. Quamvis enim ex misericordia Dei principaliter data sit eis fides tanta, tamen in quantum se præpararunt ad eam, faciendo quod in ipsis fuit, justum quodammodo fuit, seu decens et congruum, ut Deus, qui dat unicuique secundum propriam virtutem, dispositionem seu capacitatem, infunderet eis fidem tam magnam.
paras.en: Or the words [[1:1|in the justice of our God|In justitia Dei]] are to be expounded of the uncreated justice of God, so that the sense is: [[1:1|to them that have obtained equal faith with us|His qui coæqualem nobiscum sortiti sunt fidem]] [[1:1|in the justice of our God|in justitia Dei]], in that by the just judgement of God their faith was reckoned equal to our faith. And so the words [[1:1|in the justice|In justitia]] determine what he had said, [[1:1|equal|Coæqualem]] [that is, they qualify it and say in what way it is meant]. They can also determine the participle [[1:1|have obtained|Sortiti sunt]] [*sortiti sunt*, literally "have obtained by lot"], so that the sense is that by the just judgement of God such and so great a faith was given them. For although so great a faith was given them chiefly out of the mercy of God, yet inasmuch as they prepared themselves for it, doing what was in them [the schoolmen's axiom: to one who does what is in him, God does not deny grace], it was in some way just, or seemly and congruous, that God, who gives [[Matt 25:15|to every one according to his proper ability|unicuique secundum propriam virtutem]], disposition or capacity, should infuse into them so great a faith.

paras.t: Gratia vobis et pax adimpleatur, id est, perfectam gratiam plenamque pacem Deus vobis largiri dignetur, ut quantum possibile est, habeatis in vita ista pacem perfectam, loquendo de pace mentis. Sicut enim quis dicitur in vita hac esse aliquo modo perfectus in contemplatione, sapientia, caritate, ita et in pace interna. Non tamen potest pax vitæ præsentis esse indesinenter actualiterque continua. Ideo optat sanctissimus Petrus ut gratia et pax nobis adimpleatur, quatenus per gratiam et pacem viæ, ad gloriam patriæ, quæ est gratia consummata, atque ad pacem Christi, quæ exsuperat omnem sensum, quæ est pax continua nunquam finienda, post vitam hanc perducamur. Adimpleatur, inquam, in cognitione Domini nostri Jesu Christi, id est in contemplatione ipsius. Pax enim, quæ est gaudium imperturbatum, in contemplatione fundatur, et ex ea causatur, sicut et gaudium, mediante tamen dilectione, cujus gaudium et pax immediati effectus et fructus dicuntur. Siquidem Deum contemplando, non in eo gaudemus, nec in ipso mente quiescimus, nisi eum sinceriter diligamus.
paras.en: [[1:2|Grace to you and peace be accomplished|Gratia vobis et pax adimpleatur]], that is, may God deign to bestow on you perfect grace and full peace, so that, as far as is possible, you may have perfect peace in this life, speaking of peace of mind. For as a man is said to be in some way perfect in this life in contemplation, wisdom and charity, so also in inward peace. Yet the peace of the present life cannot be unceasingly and actually continuous. Therefore the most holy Peter prays that grace and peace be accomplished in us, so that through the grace and peace of the way we may be brought after this life to the glory of the fatherland, which is grace consummated, and to the peace of Christ, which surpasseth all understanding, which is a continual peace never to end [the way and the fatherland: the life of pilgrims on earth and the life of the blessed in heaven]. [[1:2|be accomplished|Adimpleatur]], I say, [[1:2|in the knowledge|in cognitione Domini nostri Jesu Christi]] of our Lord Jesus Christ [so Denis's text; the Vulgate has "of God, and of Christ Jesus our Lord"], that is, in the contemplation of him. For peace, which is undisturbed joy, is founded on contemplation and caused by it, as joy also is, yet by means of love, of which joy and peace are said to be the immediate effects and fruits. For in contemplating God we do not rejoice in him, nor rest in him with our mind, unless we love him sincerely.

paras.t: Vel, Gratia et pax adimpleatur in cognitione, id est per cognitionem, Christi, ut per eam tanquam per medium directivum, ad pacem patriæ pertingatis: juxta illud Lucæ: Illuminare his, id est, eos illumina, qui in tenebris et in umbra mortis sedent, ad dirigendos pedes, id est affectus nostros, in viam pacis.
paras.en: Or, [[1:2|Grace|Gratia]] [[1:2|and peace be accomplished|et pax adimpleatur]] [[1:2|in the knowledge|in cognitione]], that is, through the knowledge, of Christ, so that through it, as through a means that directs you, you may attain to the peace of the fatherland: according to that of Luke: [[Luke 1:79|To enlighten them|Illuminare his]], that is, enlighten them, [[Luke 1:79|that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death|qui in tenebris et in umbra mortis sedent]], [[Luke 1:79|to direct our feet|ad dirigendos pedes]], that is, our affections, [[Luke 1:79|into the way of peace|in viam pacis]].

paras.t: Insuper, quæ sequuntur, ad verba jam habita condependent, ut sit sensus: Pax vobis in Christi cognitione adimpleatur, ita ut Christo vos illustrante, etiam cognoscatis quomodo omnia nobis divinæ virtutis suæ, supple, dona sive gratiarum charismata, quæ ad vitam gratiæ jam habendam, et vitam gloriæ in futuro obtinendam, et pietatem, id est Dei cultum, seu benignitatem, vel misericordiam, (de qua loquitur Paulus: Pietas ad omnia utilis est), supple, necessaria sunt, donata sunt: hoc est, cognoscatis qualiter, quam gratiose, quam liberaliter Deus vobis donavit omnia dona gratiæ ac virtutum, quæ sunt dona ipsius divinæ virtutis, id est omnipotentiæ ejus qua ea per creationem infundit ac tribuit, quæ requiruntur et nobis sufficiunt ad bene vivendum in sæculo isto, atque ad vitam beatam adipiscendam in cœlo, et ad pietatem in omnibus exercendam, juxta illud: Exerce te ipsum ad pietatem.
paras.en: Moreover, what follows hangs on the words already given, so that the sense is: May peace be accomplished in you in the knowledge of Christ, so that, Christ enlightening you, you may also know how [[1:3|all things of his divine power|omnia nobis divinæ virtutis suæ]] (understand: the gifts, or the charisms of graces) [[1:3|which appertain to life|quæ ad vitam]] (the life of grace, to be had now, and the life of glory, to be obtained hereafter) [[1:3|and godliness|et pietatem]] [*pietas*, which the Douay-Rheims renders "godliness", means both devotion to God and kindness to others] (that is, the worship of God, or kindness, or mercy, of which Paul speaks: [[1 Tim 4:8|godliness is profitable to all things|Pietas ad omnia utilis est]]) (understand: are necessary), [[1:3|are given us|donata sunt]]: that is, that you may know in what way, how graciously, how liberally God has given you all the gifts of grace and of the virtues, which are the gifts of his divine power itself, that is, of his omnipotence, by which he infuses and bestows them by creation; which are required, and suffice us, for living well in this world, for gaining the blessed life in heaven, and for exercising godliness in all things: according to that: [[1 Tim 4:7|exercise thyself unto godliness|Exerce te ipsum ad pietatem]].

paras.t: Donata sunt autem per cognitionem ejus, id est per fidem ipsius, et per fidelem ipsius notitiam: quia per fidem creverunt ad tantam perfectionem, et Christum cognoscendo ac invocando adepti sunt charismata meliora. Vel quod ait, Per cognitionem ejus, referatur ad id quod dixerat, Quæ ad vitam et pietatem, supple, sufficiant, aut necessaria sunt: quia non nisi per Christi fidelem cognitionem dona illa sufficiant ad salutem. Oportet namque in primis fidei veritatem, et Christum per fidem cognoscere, sicque ex vera notitia ad actus virtuosos procedere.
paras.en: And they [[1:3|are given|Donata sunt]] [[1:3|through the knowledge of him|per cognitionem ejus]], that is, through faith in him and through a faithful knowledge of him: because through faith they grew to such perfection, and by knowing and calling upon Christ they obtained the better gifts. Or the words [[1:3|through the knowledge of him|Per cognitionem ejus]] may be referred to what he had said, [[1:3|which appertain to life and godliness|Quæ ad vitam et pietatem]] (understand: suffice, or are necessary): because only through a faithful knowledge of Christ do those gifts suffice for salvation. For we must first of all know the truth of the faith, and Christ, by faith, and so proceed from true knowledge to virtuous acts.

paras.t: Qui […]vit nos, id est, ad statum […]lutis apicemque virtutum perduxit, propria gloria et virtute, id est sui ipsius excellentissima majestate et omnipotentia seu in propria persona gloriosa ac omnipotente. Siquidem non legatum, non angelum, ad redimendum nos misit, sed ipsemet venit, et salvos nos fecit: et hoc, per assumptam humanitatem, quæ salvandi efficaciam habuit a virtute increata divinitatis, cui totum est principaliter adscribendum, juxta illud Isaiæ: Dominus judex noster, Dominus legifer noster; ipse veniet et salvabit nos. De quo loquitur evangelicus Zacharias: Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel, quia visitavit et fecit redemptionem plebis suæ.
paras.en: Who hath […] us, that is, hath brought us to the state of […] and to the summit of the virtues, [[1:3|by his own proper glory and virtue|propria gloria et virtute]], that is, by his own most excellent majesty and omnipotence, or in his own glorious and almighty Person. For he sent not an envoy, not an angel, to redeem us, but came himself and saved us: and this through the humanity he assumed, which had its power to save from the uncreated might of the Godhead, to which the whole is chiefly to be ascribed; according to that of Isaias: [[Is 33:22|the Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver|Dominus judex noster, Dominus legifer noster]]; [[Is 35:4|God himself will come and will save you|ipse veniet et salvabit nos]] [Denis reads "will save us", as in Is 33:22]. Of him the evangelical Zachary speaks: [[Luke 1:68|Blessed be the Lord God of Israel: because he hath visited and wrought the redemption of his people.|Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel, quia visitavit et fecit redemptionem plebis suæ]]

paras.t: Per quem, scilicet Jesum Christum; ut alii habent, Per quam, videlicet Christi fidelem cognitionem; maxima et pretiosa nobis promissa donavit, id est, excellentissima dona Spiritus Sancti et munera pretiosissima, tam gratiæ gratis datæ, quam gratiæ gratum facientis, præsertim in die Pentecostes, quando in visibili signo […]piosissime datus est Spiritus Sanctus […] infusionem munerum ejus: quæ Christus tam in veteri Testamento per Prophetas, quam per se ipsum in sermone quem […]cit post Cœnam, danda prænuntiavit atque spopondit. Prædixit quippe per Joelem: Effundam de Spiritu meo super omnem carnem, et prophetabunt filii vestri et filiæ vestræ. Et in Psalmo: Dominus dabit verbum evangelizantibus virtute multa; accepisti dona in hominibus; Deus Israel ipse dabit virtutem et fortitudinem plebi suæ. Christus quoque ait: Paracletus Spiritus Sanctus, quem mittet Pater in nomine meo, ille vos docebit omnia, et suggeret vobis omnia quæcumque dixero vobis. Ascensurus autem ad cælum, dixit eis: Sedete in civitate quoadusque induamini virtute ex alto, et eam nullam […]
paras.en: [[1:4|By whom|Per quem]], namely Jesus Christ; or, as others have it, By which [*per quam*, which would refer to the knowledge spoken of in v. 3], namely the faithful knowledge of Christ, [[1:4|he hath given us most great and precious promises|maxima et pretiosa nobis promissa donavit]], that is, the most excellent gifts of the Holy Ghost and most precious bounties, both of grace freely given and of sanctifying grace [*gratia gratis data*, grace given for the good of others, such as prophecy; *gratia gratum faciens*, the grace that makes the soul itself pleasing to God], above all on the day of Pentecost[[Acts 2:1||]], when the Holy Ghost was given most […]piously in a visible sign […] the infusion of his gifts: which Christ foretold and promised would be given, both in the Old Testament through the Prophets and in his own person in the discourse which he […] after the Supper. For he foretold through Joel: [[Joel 2:28|I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh: and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy|Effundam de Spiritu meo super omnem carnem, et prophetabunt filii vestri et filiæ vestræ]]. And in the Psalm: [[Ps 67:12|The Lord shall give the word to them that preach good tidings with great power|Dominus dabit verbum evangelizantibus virtute multa]]; [[Ps 67:19|thou hast received gifts in men|accepisti dona in hominibus]]; [[Ps 67:36|the God of Israel is he who will give power and strength to his people|Deus Israel ipse dabit virtutem et fortitudinem plebi suæ]] [the margin reads Ps. lxxxvi, 12, 13; the words are Ps 67:12, 19 and 36]. Christ also says: [[John 14:26|the Paraclete, the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring all things to your mind, whatsoever I shall have said to you|Paracletus Spiritus Sanctus, quem mittet Pater in nomine meo, ille vos docebit omnia, et suggeret vobis omnia quæcumque dixero vobis]]. And when about to ascend into heaven, he said to them: [[Luke 24:49|stay you in the city till you be endued with power from on high|Sedete in civitate quoadusque induamini virtute ex alto]], and it no […]

paras.t: […] naturæ, id est, per hæc supernaturalia gratiæ dona Deo supernaturaliter conformemini, et tandem ad plenam cum Deo assimilationem pertingatis in patria. Quum enim sit homo ad summæ Trinitatis imaginem similitudinemque productus, et per consequens, per dona naturæ aliqualiter consors divinæ naturæ, seu particeps perfectionis ac bonitatis proprii Creatoris: certum est quod per dona gratiæ altiori perfectiorique modo Deo assimiletur, quia dona naturæ perficiuntur a donis gratiæ.
paras.en: […] [[1:4|nature|naturæ]], that is, that through these supernatural gifts of grace you may be supernaturally conformed to God, and at last attain to full likeness with God in the fatherland. For since man was made to the image and likeness of the most high Trinity, and consequently, through the gifts of nature, is in some way a partaker of the divine nature, that is, a sharer in the perfection and goodness of his own Creator, it is certain that through the gifts of grace he is likened to God in a higher and more perfect way, because the gifts of nature are perfected by the gifts of grace.

paras.t: Et quo dona gratiæ fuerint eminentiora, eo sublimius dicuntur hominem Deo conformare, eumque deificare, seu divinum ac deiformem efficere: non quod esse creatum amittat, et induat esse increatum; sed quia per dona, virtutes ac habitus supernaturales, eminentes, perfectos, eorumque actus assiduos et præclaros, valde supernaturaliter, mirabiliter ac gratiosissime Creatori reddatur conformis. Et istud fit maxime per caritatem ardentem et sapientiæ donum, et actus ex eis procedentes; deinde per alia dona ac virtutes, eorumque actus, secundum quod insunt viris heroicis et perfectis. Unumquodque siquidem dicitur ei potissimum conformari, atque cum illo quasi societatem et communionem habere, cujus opera magis exsequitur, et cui in actibus suis amplius assimilatur. Propter quod homines carnales dicuntur brutales, et luxuriosi dicuntur porcini.
paras.en: And the more eminent the gifts of grace are, the more sublimely they are said to conform a man to God and to deify him, that is, to make him divine and deiform: not that he loses his created being and puts on uncreated being, but because through supernatural, eminent and perfect gifts, virtues and habits, and their constant and splendid acts, he is made conformable to his Creator very supernaturally, wonderfully and most graciously. And this comes about chiefly through ardent charity and the gift of wisdom, and the acts that proceed from them; then through the other gifts and virtues and their acts, according as they are found in heroic and perfect men. For each thing is said to be conformed above all to that, and to have as it were fellowship and communion with that, whose works it most carries out and which it most resembles in its acts. For this reason carnal men are called brutish, and the lustful swinish.

paras.t: Merito igitur qui actibus virtuosis insistunt, qui actionibus intellectualium virium (in quibus summæ Trinitatis imago resplendet) intenti sunt, qui contemplando, ferventer amando, pietatem et justitiam exercendo, se Deo conformant, et spiritualem, internam cælestemque vitam ducunt in terra, divinæ naturæ consortes sive participes effici, Dei quoque amici ac filii fieri. Filiorum namque est, suo patri assimilari; et amicitia in quadam communione fundatur. Et isti familiares effecti sunt. Habent, inquam, societatem cum Deo, quia hoc agunt quod ipse, veritatem amando ac contemplando, aliosque actus divinos ac Deo placitos exercendo, et ei intenti sunt, ejusque perfectionem et beatitudinem aliquo modo participant: per quæ omnia Deo assimilantur. Hæc vero communio, assimilatio atque conjunctio, consortium seu societatem efficiunt. Propter quod in Ecclesiastico dicitur: Omnis homo simili sibi associabitur; et in prima Joannis Canonica habetur, Societas vestra sit cum Patre et Filio ejus Jesu Christo. Et quia communio, assimilatio et unio jam præfatæ cum Deo, multo perfectius habentur in patria quam in via, idcirco electi et Sancti, dicuntur Deo in cœlo perfecte assimilari et consociari. Propter quod in prima sua Canonica scribit Joannes: Similes ei erimus, quia videbimus eum sicuti est. Et alio loco idem Joannes asserit: Quotquot receperunt eum, dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri. Quod exponitur de filiatione perfecta, quæ habetur per similitudinem gloriæ, per quam electi fiunt præcipue consortes divinæ naturæ, et societatem sortiuntur cum Deo, ejus beatitudinem usque ad satietatem participantes, et ipsomet Deo beatifice perfruentes, quo et nunc per dona gratiæ aliqualiter fruimur, ei propter se inhærendo, atque ad eum alia cuncta finaliter referendo.
paras.en: Rightly, then, are those who apply themselves to virtuous acts, who are intent on the acts of the intellectual powers (in which the image of the most high Trinity shines forth), who conform themselves to God by contemplating, by loving fervently, by exercising godliness and justice, and who lead on earth a spiritual, inward and heavenly life, said to be made [[1:4|partakers of the divine nature|divinæ naturæ consortes]], or sharers in it, and to become also friends and sons of God. For it belongs to sons to be like their father; and friendship is founded on a certain communion. And these have been made God's intimates. They have, I say, fellowship with God, because they do what he does, loving and contemplating the truth and performing other acts that are divine and pleasing to God, and are intent on him, and in some way share in his perfection and beatitude: by all of which they are likened to God. And this communion, likeness and union make a consortship or fellowship [*consortium*, the word behind Peter's *consortes*, "partakers"]. For this reason it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 13:20|every man shall associate himself to his like|Omnis homo simili sibi associabitur]] [the margin gives Ecclus. viii, 20; the words are at Ecclus 13:20]; and in the first canonical epistle of John we have: [[1 John 1:3|our fellowship may be with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ|Societas vestra sit cum Patre et Filio ejus Jesu Christo]] [Denis reads *vestra*, "your" fellowship]. And because the communion, likeness and union with God already spoken of are had far more perfectly in the fatherland than on the way, therefore the elect and the Saints are said to be perfectly likened to God and joined in fellowship with him in heaven. For this reason John writes in his first canonical epistle: [[1 John 3:2|we shall be like to him: because we shall see him as he is|Similes ei erimus, quia videbimus eum sicuti est]]. And in another place the same John declares: [[John 1:12|as many as received him, he gave them power to be made the sons of God|Quotquot receperunt eum, dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri]]. This is expounded of perfect sonship, which is had through the likeness of glory, by which the elect are made above all partakers of the divine nature and obtain fellowship with God, sharing his beatitude to the full, and enjoying God himself in bliss; whom even now we in some way enjoy through the gifts of grace, cleaving to him for his own sake and referring all other things to him as their end.

paras.t: Denique præinductam hanc beatissimi Petri sententiam de maximis et pretiosis donis desuper nobis collatis, et cognitione, ponit et Paulus ad Ephesios, dicens: Pater gloriæ det vobis spiritum sapientiæ, ut sciatis quæ sit spes vocationis ejus, et quæ divitiæ gloriæ hereditatis ejus in Sanctis, et quæ sit supereminens magnitudo virtutis ejus in nos qui credidimus.
paras.en: Lastly, this sentence of the most blessed Peter just brought forward, on the most great and precious gifts bestowed on us from above, and on knowledge, Paul also sets down to the Ephesians, saying: [[Eph 1:17|the Father of glory, may give unto you the spirit of wisdom|Pater gloriæ det vobis spiritum sapientiæ]], [[Eph 1:18|that you may know what the hope is of his calling and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints|ut sciatis quæ sit spes vocationis ejus, et quæ divitiæ gloriæ hereditatis ejus in Sanctis]], [[Eph 1:19|And what is the exceeding greatness of his power towards us, who believe|et quæ sit supereminens magnitudo virtutis ejus in nos qui credidimus]].

paras.t: Sic ergo, Efficiamini divinæ consortes naturæ, fugientes ejus quæ in mundo est concupiscentiæ corruptionem, id est vitiositatem et infectionem mundanæ ac carnalis concupiscentiæ, cupiditatis, libidinis, et omnis inordinatæ affectionis, quæ spiritualiter corrumpit ac destruit hominem; sed et cetera peccata mortalia, quoniam omni spirituali esse gratiæ ac virtutum spoliant eum. Hujus concupiscentiæ corruptionem fugimus, concupiscentiæ non consentiendo, sed eam frenando ac repellendo, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Quasi a facie colubri fuge peccata. Nam sicut fugimus serpentes inficere nos volentes, sic fugere nos oportet concupiscentias corrumpentes: imo tanto plus, quo deterior est spiritualis quam corporalis interitus. Hæc corruptio opponitur sanitati interiori, seu integritati virtutum, qua homo tota mente Deo adhæret absque divisione, ita quod non partim mundo.
paras.en: So then, [[1:4|you may be made partakers of the divine nature|Efficiamini divinæ consortes naturæ]], [[1:4|flying the corruption of that concupiscence which is in the world|fugientes ejus quæ in mundo est concupiscentiæ corruptionem]], that is, the viciousness and infection of worldly and carnal concupiscence, of covetousness, of lust, and of every disordered affection, which spiritually corrupts and destroys a man; and also the other mortal sins, since they strip him of all the spiritual being of grace and of the virtues. We fly the corruption of this concupiscence by not consenting to concupiscence, but bridling and repelling it, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 21:2|Flee from sins as from the face of a serpent|Quasi a facie colubri fuge peccata]]. For as we fly from serpents that would infect us, so we must fly the concupiscences that corrupt us: nay, so much the more, as spiritual death is worse than bodily. This corruption is opposed to inward health, or the integrity of the virtues, by which a man cleaves to God with his whole mind, without division, so that he does not belong partly to the world.

paras.t: Præterea recte ait, Ejus quæ in mundo est concupiscentiæ corruptionem. Est enim et alia concupiscentia spiritualis et munda, videlicet desiderium Dei et sapientiæ ac virtutum, quæ non est in mundo, id est mundanis hominibus, sed in virtuosis, de quibus ait Salvator: De mundo non estis. De qua concupiscentia in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Auris bona cum omni concupiscentia audiet sapientiam; et Psalmista, Concupiscit et deficit anima mea in atria Domini. Unde Sapientia: Concupiscentia (inquit) sapientiæ deducit ad regnum perpetuum. Hæc concupiscentia parit incorruptionem, de qua fertur ibidem: Incorruptio facit esse proximum Deo.
paras.en: Moreover he rightly says, [[1:4|the corruption of that concupiscence which is in the world|Ejus quæ in mundo est concupiscentiæ corruptionem]]. For there is also another concupiscence, spiritual and clean, namely the desire of God, of wisdom and of the virtues, which is not in the world, that is, in worldly men, but in the virtuous, of whom the Saviour says: [[John 15:19|you are not of the world|De mundo non estis]]. Of this concupiscence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 3:31|a good ear will hear wisdom with all desire|Auris bona cum omni concupiscentia audiet sapientiam]] [*concupiscentia*: "desire" here is the same Latin word as "concupiscence"]; and the Psalmist: [[Ps 83:3|my soul longeth and fainteth for the courts of the Lord|Concupiscit et deficit anima mea in atria Domini]]. Hence Wisdom says: [[Wis 6:21|the desire|Concupiscentia]] (it says) [[Wis 6:21|of wisdom bringeth to the everlasting kingdom|sapientiæ deducit ad regnum perpetuum]]. This concupiscence brings forth incorruption, of which it is said in the same place: [[Wis 6:20|incorruption bringeth near to God|Incorruptio facit esse proximum Deo]].

paras.t: Sed quia in vita præsenti oportet semper proficere, otiositatem vitare, tempus omne fructuose expendere, recte subjungitur: Vos autem curam omnem subinferentes, id est, omnem spiritualem sollicitudinem seu diligentiam apponentes, et ab intimo corde introducentes, ac assumentes ad virtuose vivendum, ministrate, id est, ministerialiter exercete. Deus enim est auctor principalis omnis operis boni; homo autem tanquam Dei minister et instrumentum, agit sive exsequitur id ad quod a Deo movetur. Propter quod loquitur Paulus: Deus operatur in vobis velle et perficere; itemque, Dei cooperatores sumus. Quia tamen libere facimus istud, reputatur nobis in meritum, quamvis sit Dei donum.
paras.en: But because in the present life we must always make progress, shun idleness and spend all our time fruitfully, there rightly follows: [[1:5|And you, employing all care|Vos autem curam omnem subinferentes]], that is, applying all spiritual solicitude or diligence, bringing it in from the inmost heart and taking it up for living virtuously, [[1:5|minister|ministrate]], that is, exercise it as ministers [that is, as servants and instruments, as he goes on to say]. For God is the principal author of every good work; but man, as God's minister and instrument, does or carries out that to which he is moved by God. For this reason Paul says: [[Phil 2:13|God who worketh in you, both to will and to accomplish|Deus operatur in vobis velle et perficere]]; and again, [[1 Cor 3:9|we are God's coadjutors|Dei cooperatores sumus]] [no margin reference; Denis's wording differs a little from the Vulgate's *Dei enim sumus adjutores*]. Yet because we do this freely, it is reckoned to us as merit, though it is God's gift.

paras.t: Itaque, Ministrate et facite in fide vestra virtutem, id est opera virtuosa, quoniam fides sine operibus mortua est in se ipsa. Et istud cum omni agendum est cura, quoniam Salomone testante, Qui mollis et dissolutus est in opere suo, frater est sua opera dissipantis. Apud Jeremiam quoque inducitur: Maledictus qui facit opus Dei negligenter. Ideo admonet Paulus: Serviamus Deo cum metu et reverentia; et rursus, Cum timore, inquit, et tremore vestram salutem operamini. In virtute autem scientiam, id est discretionem, quæ est directrix et auriga virtutum, docens observare moderamen, congruum locum, tempusque aptum, ut omnia ordinate agantur, et regia via tendamus, ut sit rationabile obsequium nostrum. Ideo dicitur in Isaia: Discite bene agere.
paras.en: So: [[1:5|minister|Ministrate]] and do [[1:5|in your faith, virtue|in fide vestra virtutem]], that is, virtuous works, since faith without works [[Jas 2:17|is dead in itself|mortua est in se ipsa]]. And this is to be done with all care, since, as Solomon bears witness, [[Prov 18:9|He that is loose and slack in his work, is the brother of him that wasteth his own works.|Qui mollis et dissolutus est in opere suo, frater est sua opera dissipantis]] In Jeremias too it is set down: [[Jer 48:10|Cursed be he that doth the work of the Lord deceitfully|Maledictus qui facit opus Dei negligenter]] [Denis reads *negligenter*, "negligently", where the Vulgate has *fraudulenter*, "deceitfully"]. Therefore Paul admonishes: [[Heb 12:28|let us serve, pleasing God, with fear and reverence|Serviamus Deo cum metu et reverentia]]; and again, [[Phil 2:12|with fear|Cum timore]], he says, [[Phil 2:12|and trembling work out your salvation|et tremore vestram salutem operamini]]. [[1:5|And in virtue, knowledge|In virtute autem scientiam]], that is, discretion, which is the guide and charioteer of the virtues, teaching us to keep measure, the fitting place and the apt time, so that all things may be done in order and we may go by the royal road, so that it may be our [[Rom 12:1|reasonable service|rationabile obsequium nostrum]]. Therefore it is said in Isaias: [[Is 1:17|Learn to do well|Discite bene agere]].

paras.t: In scientia autem habete, ministrate, seu exercete, abstinentiam, a carnalibus voluptatibus vos reprimendo, præsertim a delectabilibus gustus et tactus, et vitia gulæ atque luxuriæ fugiatis, juxta illud ad Thessalonicenses: Hæc est voluntas Dei, sanctificatio vestra, ut abstineatis vos a fornicatione, ut sciat unusquisque vestrum suum vas (id est proprium corpus) possidere in sanctificatione et honore, non in passione desiderii, sicut et gentes quæ ignorant Deum. In abstinentia autem patientiam: quæ castis et sobriis, suumque corpus castigantibus, valde est necessaria, ne ex corporali afflictione ad impatientiam sive tristitiam moveantur. Propter quod ait Salvator: Quum jejunatis, nolite fieri, sicut hypocritæ, tristes; tu autem quum jejunas, unge caput tuum, et faciem tuam lava. Hinc ad Hebræos fertur: Patientia vobis necessaria est, ut voluntatem Dei facientes, reportetis promissionem. In patientia autem pietatem, ne sitis circa alios nimium rigidi, sed condescendentes. Solent enim nonnulli, qui sibi ipsis rigorosi sunt, etiam aliis duri esse, non satis compassivi et succurrentes. Iterum, non sufficit adversa illata ab aliis, patienter sufferre, nisi et illis caritatis ac pietatis impendamus affectum, et oremus pro ipsis, quum dicat Salvator: Benefacite his qui oderunt vos, et orate pro persequentibus et calumniantibus vos.
paras.en: [[1:6|And in knowledge|In scientia autem]] have, minister or exercise [[1:6|abstinence|abstinentiam]], restraining yourselves from carnal pleasures, especially from the delights of taste and touch, and fleeing the vices of gluttony and lust; according to that to the Thessalonians: [[1 Thess 4:3|this is the will of God, your sanctification: That you should abstain from fornication|Hæc est voluntas Dei, sanctificatio vestra, ut abstineatis vos a fornicatione]]: [[1 Thess 4:4|That every one of you should know how to possess his vessel|ut sciat unusquisque vestrum suum vas]] (that is, his own body) [[1 Thess 4:4|in sanctification and honour|possidere in sanctificatione et honore]], [[1 Thess 4:5|Not in the passion of lust, like the Gentiles that know not God:|non in passione desiderii, sicut et gentes quæ ignorant Deum]] [[1:6|and in abstinence, patience|In abstinentia autem patientiam]]: which is very necessary for the chaste and sober, who chastise their bodies, lest from bodily affliction they be moved to impatience or sadness. For this reason the Saviour says: [[Matt 6:16|when you fast, be not as the hypocrites, sad|Quum jejunatis, nolite fieri, sicut hypocritæ, tristes]]; [[Matt 6:17|But thou, when thou fastest anoint thy head, and wash thy face|tu autem quum jejunas, unge caput tuum, et faciem tuam lava]]. Hence it is said to the Hebrews: [[Heb 10:36|patience is necessary for you: that, doing the will of God, you may receive the promise|Patientia vobis necessaria est, ut voluntatem Dei facientes, reportetis promissionem]]. [[1:6|and in patience, godliness|In patientia autem pietatem]], so that you be not too rigid towards others, but condescending [that is, bending kindly to their weakness]. For some who are rigorous with themselves are wont to be hard on others too, not compassionate and helpful enough. Again, it is not enough to bear patiently the adversities brought on us by others, unless we also show them an affection of charity and kindness, and pray for them, since the Saviour says: [[Matt 5:44|do good to them that hate you: and pray for them that persecute and calumniate you|Benefacite his qui oderunt vos, et orate pro persequentibus et calumniantibus vos]].

paras.t: In pietate autem amorem fraternitatis, id est, fraternam dilectionem habete, quatenus opera pietatis ex vera et fraternali exhibeatis dilectione. In amore autem fraternitatis caritatem, id est, Dei dilectionem habeatis sinceram: quoniam caritas Dei, ceterarum virtutum vita et forma, vertex et finis, regina et motrix est. Et amor fraternus, Dei amore est condiendus, formandus ac perficiendus, atque ad Dei actualem dilectionem finaliter referendus. Propter quod ad Colossenses dicitur: Super omnia caritatem habete, quod est vinculum perfectionis.
paras.en: [[1:7|And in godliness, love of brotherhood|In pietate autem amorem fraternitatis]], that is, have brotherly love, so that you may show the works of godliness out of a true and brotherly love. [[1:7|and in love of brotherhood, charity|In amore autem fraternitatis caritatem]], that is, have a sincere love of God: since the charity of God is the life and form, the summit and end, the queen and mover of the other virtues. And brotherly love is to be seasoned, formed and perfected by the love of God, and referred in the end to the actual love of God [that is, to the love of God as actually exercised]. For this reason it is said to the Colossians: [[Col 3:14|above all these things have charity, which is the bond of perfection|Super omnia caritatem habete, quod est vinculum perfectionis]].

paras.t: His octo virtutibus, tanquam per octo gradus, ad felicitatem et cœlestem Jerusalem ascenditur ac pervenitur. Ad quod præsignandum, in visione Ezechielis de templo asseritur, quod per octo gradus ascendebatur ad ipsum. Et Psalmista loquitur Deo de homine virtuoso: Beatus vir cujus est auxilium abs te, ascensiones in corde suo disposuit. Et subditur ibi: Ibunt de virtute in virtutem, videbitur Deus deorum in Sion.
paras.en: By these eight virtues, as by eight steps, one ascends and comes to happiness and the heavenly Jerusalem. To foreshadow this, it is said in Ezechiel's vision of the temple that it was reached by eight steps[[Ezech 40:31||]][[Ezech 40:49||]]. And the Psalmist speaks to God of the virtuous man: [[Ps 83:6|Blessed is the man whose help is from thee: in his heart he hath disposed to ascend by steps|Beatus vir cujus est auxilium abs te, ascensiones in corde suo disposuit]]. And there follows: [[Ps 83:8|they shall go from virtue to virtue: the God of gods shall be seen in Sion|Ibunt de virtute in virtutem, videbitur Deus deorum in Sion]].

paras.t: Hæc enim, id est hæ præfatæ octo virtutes, si vobiscum adsint, id est, cordibus vestris semper inhæreant, et superent, id est, vitia sibi opposita vincant; vel, Superent, id est, invalescant atque abundent; non vacuos, nec sine fructu vos constituent in Domini nostri Jesu Christi cognitione. Minus dicit, et majus significat, ut sit sensus: Prædictæ virtutes plenos meritoriis actibus vos efficient, et in regno cœlesti vos exaltabunt in aperta ac beatifica divinitatis Christi visione. De qua idem ait: Hæc est vita æterna, ut cognoscant te verum Deum, et quem misisti Jesum Christum; et alibi, Manifestabo ei me ipsum.
paras.en: [[1:8|For if these things|Hæc enim]], that is, these eight virtues aforesaid, [[1:8|be with you|si vobiscum adsint]], that is, ever cleave to your hearts, [[1:8|and abound|et superent]], that is, overcome the vices opposed to them; or, [[1:8|abound|Superent]], that is, grow strong and abound [the Latin *superent* means both "overcome" and "be over and above, abound"]; [[1:8|they will make you to be neither empty nor unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ|non vacuos, nec sine fructu vos constituent in Domini nostri Jesu Christi cognitione]]. He says less and means more [the figure called litotes], so that the sense is: The aforesaid virtues will make you full of meritorious acts, and will exalt you in the heavenly kingdom in the open and beatific vision of the Godhead of Christ. Of which he himself says: [[John 17:3|this is eternal life: That they may know thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent|Hæc est vita æterna, ut cognoscant te verum Deum, et quem misisti Jesum Christum]]; and elsewhere: I [[John 14:21|will manifest myself to him|Manifestabo ei me ipsum]].

paras.t: Cui enim non præsto sunt hæc, cæcus est, id est, mente obtenebratus, utpote infidelis et indiscretus, et manu tentans, id est, quo eat ignorans, nec qualiter ad beatitudinem progredi debeat sciens. Ideo similis est cæco qui manu extenta tentat et scire conatur quo tendere debeat. Idcirco mox cadit in præceps, et peccat, ac perit. Propterea, teste Ambrosio, ignorantia est maximum vitiorum, non utique magnitudine enormitatis, sed periculositatis, quum in primis scire oporteat qualiter sit vivendum. Propter quod ait et Paulus: Qui ignorat, ignorabitur. Et apud Baruch scriptum est: Disce ubi sit sapientia, ubi sit virtus, ubi sit intellectus, ut scias ubi sit longiturnitas vitæ, ubi sit lumen oculorum et pax. Oblivionem accipiens purgationis veterum suorum delictorum, id est, peccata sua pristina et antiqua purgare et emendare obliviscitur, negligit, seu omittit; et si baptizatus est, per negligentiam suam ostendit se esse oblitum purgationis quam in Baptismo accepit, quoniam tantum Dei beneficium non attendit, nec gratias agit Deo.
paras.en: [[1:9|For he that hath not these things with him|Cui enim non præsto sunt hæc]], that is, he to whom the aforesaid virtues are not present, [[1:9|is blind|cæcus est]], that is, darkened in mind, as being unbelieving and without discretion, [[1:9|and groping|et manu tentans]] [literally "trying with the hand"], that is, not knowing where he goes, nor knowing how he ought to advance to beatitude. He is therefore like a blind man who feels about with outstretched hand and tries to learn which way he should go. And so he soon falls headlong, and sins, and perishes. Therefore, as Ambrose witnesses, ignorance is the greatest of vices, not indeed by the greatness of its enormity but by its danger, since we must first of all know how we are to live. For this reason Paul too says: [[1 Cor 14:38|if any man know not, he shall not be known|Qui ignorat, ignorabitur]]. And in Baruch it is written: [[Bar 3:14|Learn where is wisdom, where is strength, where is understanding: that thou mayst know also where is length of days and life, where is the light of the eyes, and peace|Disce ubi sit sapientia, ubi sit virtus, ubi sit intellectus, ut scias ubi sit longiturnitas vitæ, ubi sit lumen oculorum et pax]]. [[1:9|having forgotten that he was purged from his old sins|Oblivionem accipiens purgationis veterum suorum delictorum]], that is, he forgets, neglects or omits to cleanse and amend his former and old sins; and if he is baptized, he shows by his negligence that he has forgotten the cleansing he received in Baptism, since he pays no heed to so great a benefit of God, and gives no thanks to God.

paras.t: Quapropter, o fratres, magis satagite, id est, diligentius insistite et studete, ut per bona opera certam vestram vocationem et electionem faciatis, id est, vos ipsos in primis, et quodammodo alios certificetis, vos esse a Deo ad statum gratiæ ac salutis vocatos, deductos, atque ab ipso electos, seu æternaliter prædestinatos. Hoc enim suo modo agnoscitur, si quis Creatori serviat diligenter, peccata abhorreat, Deo semper placere intendat, desideret et conetur, ac perseveret in bonis.
paras.en: [[1:10|Wherefore, brethren, labour the more|Quapropter, o fratres, magis satagite]], that is, apply yourselves and strive more diligently, [[1:10|that by good works you may make sure your calling and election|ut per bona opera certam vestram vocationem et electionem faciatis]]: that is, that you may make sure, first of all to yourselves and in some fashion to others, that you have been called by God to the state of grace and salvation, led to it, and chosen by him, or predestined from eternity. For this is known, in its own way, if a man serves the Creator diligently, abhors sins, always intends, desires and strives to please God, and perseveres in good works.

paras.t: Posset hic quæri, an quis in vita hac certitudinaliter scire valeat, se esse in caritate et gratia, seu esse electum. Et possent pro utraque parte multæ ex Scripturis auctoritates, et ex verbis Sanctorum allegari. Sed prolixitatem vitando (quia hæc quæstio alibi copiose invenitur discussa), in hoc stat vis responsionis, secundum doctores præcipuos, quod tanta est conformitas amoris naturalis acquisiti, et amoris infusi, ceterarumque virtutum infusarum et acquisitarum, inter se et in actibus suis, quod nemo absque divina revelatione certitudinaliter scire potest ex quibuscumque actibus suis, se esse in caritate et gratia : quamvis conjecturaliter posset hoc scire, et probabiliter valde ; alioqui periculose agerent sacerdotes devoti assidue celebrando. Et quanto quis in virtutibus amplius proficit, tanto probabilius potest cognoscere se esse in caritate. Sed et Spiritus Sanctus testimonium perhibet spiritui nostro, quod filii Dei sumus : quod tamen testimonium diversimode potest intelligi, et multipliciter perhiberi. Nec verum est quod quidam scribit hoc loco, dicens, Eo ipso quod aliquis est in gratia, oportet quod sit vocatus et electus : si de electo sit proprie sermo, secundum quod ait Salvator : Multi vocati, pauci electi. Multi etenim reprobi et præsciti, sunt ad tempus in gratia.
paras.en: Here it might be asked whether anyone in this life can know with certainty that he is in charity and grace, or that he is one of the elect. And many authorities from the Scriptures and from the words of the Saints could be brought forward on either side. But to avoid length (since this question is found discussed at large elsewhere), the force of the answer, according to the chief doctors, lies in this: so great is the likeness between natural, acquired love and infused love, and among the other virtues, infused and acquired, both in themselves and in their acts, that no one without a divine revelation can know with certainty, from any acts of his whatever, that he is in charity and grace; though he can know it by conjecture, and with great probability: otherwise devout priests would act dangerously in celebrating [that is, saying Mass, which must be done in the state of grace] day after day. And the more a man advances in the virtues, the more probably can he know that he is in charity. But the Holy Ghost also [[Rom 8:16|giveth testimony to our spirit that we are the sons of God|testimonium perhibet spiritui nostro, quod filii Dei sumus]]; which testimony, however, can be understood in different ways, and be given in many ways. Nor is it true, what someone writes on this place, saying: By the very fact that a man is in grace, he must be called and chosen; if we are speaking of the elect in the proper sense, according to what the Saviour says: [[Matt 22:14|many are called, but few are chosen|Multi vocati, pauci electi]][[Matt 20:16||]]. For many of the reprobate and foreknown [that is, those whom God foresees will not persevere to salvation] are in grace for a time.

paras.t: Unde quod princeps Apostolorum hic ait, Per bona opera certam faciatis vocationem vestram et electionem, valde pensandum est : quia videtur innuere, quod per bona opera posset quis certificare se quod sit electus. Quocirca sciendum, quod eo modo quo per quotidiana opera bona certi efficimus quod sumus de facto vel in præsentiarum in gratia, ita perseverando in eis, certificamur de nostra electione. Sed utraque certificatio intelligenda est, non de certitudine absoluta, qualis habetur in mathematicis, sed de certitudine verisimili, conjecturali, probabili, quæ habetur in moralibus. Unde Aristoteles Boetiusque affirmant, quod sensati ac disciplinati viri est, in omni materia certitudinem quærere, prout materia sustinet, et natura rei admittit. Idcirco et sapientissimus Archiapostolus loquitur modo de certitudine hujusmodi, quæ in genere seu proposito isto atque materia hac potest haberi.
paras.en: Hence what the prince of the Apostles says here, [[1:10|by good works you may make sure your calling and election|Per bona opera certam faciatis vocationem vestram et electionem]], is to be weighed carefully: for he seems to hint that by good works a man could make himself sure that he is one of the elect. Wherefore it must be known that, in the way in which by daily good works we are made sure that we are in fact, or at present, in grace, so by persevering in them we are made sure of our election. But each assurance is to be understood not of absolute certainty, such as is had in mathematics, but of a likely, conjectural, probable certainty, such as is had in moral matters. Hence Aristotle and Boethius affirm that it is the mark of a sensible and well-schooled man to seek certainty in every matter so far as the matter bears it and the nature of the thing admits. Therefore the most wise Archapostle too speaks here of the sort of certainty that can be had in this kind or subject and in this matter.

paras.t: Hæc enim facientes, id est, per opera virtuosa certam vestram vocationem electionemque facientes, non peccabitis aliquando. Hoc tripliciter potest intelligi : Primo, quia sic conversando, ad æternam beatitudinem pertingetis, in qua nunquam peccabitis. Secundo, quia manendo in gratia, non peccabitis, quum peccatum contingat gratiam amittendo, vel ab ejus perfectione deficiendo. Sicque in prima Joannis Canonica fertur : Qui manet in eo, non peccat. Tertio, quia hæc faciendo, homo meditatur novissima sua, quorum meditatio frequens expellit peccata, secundum illud Ecclesiastici : In omnibus operibus tuis memorare novissima tua, et in æternum non peccabis. Itaque, Non peccabitis, loquendo de peccatis mortalibus. Nam venialia prorsus vitare non potest homo in hac vita fragili : quorum etsi singula, non tamen omnia queunt vitari, eo quod quum homo intentus est vitare unum, subito ex fragilitate et instabilitate propriæ mentis, incidat in aliud. Propter quod tertio Regum habetur, Non est homo super terram, qui faciat bonum, et non peccet : quoniam ipsis bonis operibus venialia se commiscent.
paras.en: [[1:10|For doing these things|Hæc enim facientes]], that is, making your calling and election sure through works of virtue, [[1:10|you shall not sin at any time|non peccabitis aliquando]]. This can be understood in three ways. First, because by living so you will attain eternal beatitude, in which you will never sin. Secondly, because by remaining in grace you will not sin, since sin comes about by losing grace or by falling short of its perfection. And so it is said in the first Canonical Epistle of John: [[1 John 3:6|Whosoever abideth in him sinneth not|Qui manet in eo, non peccat]]. Thirdly, because in doing these things a man meditates on his last things, the frequent meditation of which drives out sins, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 7:40|In all thy works remember thy last end, and thou shalt never sin|In omnibus operibus tuis memorare novissima tua, et in æternum non peccabis]] [the margin gives Ecclus. xviii, 40; the verse is Ecclus 7:40]. And so, [[1:10|you shall not sin|Non peccabitis]] is said of mortal sins. For venial sins man cannot altogether avoid in this frail life: though each of them singly can be avoided, not all of them can, because while a man is intent on avoiding one, he suddenly falls into another out of the frailty and instability of his own mind. For which reason it is said in the third book of Kings: There is no man upon earth that doth good and sinneth not[[3 Kings 8:46||]][[Eccles 7:21||]] [3 Kings 8:46 has only "there is no man who sinneth not"; Denis's fuller wording is that of Eccles 7:21, "there is no just man upon earth, that doth good, and sinneth not"]: since venial sins mingle with our very good works.

paras.t: Deinde subjungitur alia ratio, cur sic agere debeamus. Sic enim abundanter ministrabitur vobis introitus, id est, prompte et copiose præstabitur vobis a Judice summo facultas intrandi, in æternum regnum Domini nostri et Salvatoris Jesu Christi, cujus regni non erit finis. De quo in Daniele scribitur : Potestas ejus potestas æterna, quæ non auferetur, et regnum ejus quod non corrumpetur; atque in Psalmo, Regnum tuum, regnum omnium sæculorum. Vel, Ministrabitur vobis abundanter introitus in regnum Christi, quia sic faciendo, proficietis quotidie in omni gratia ac virtute, et abundabitis meritis, per quæ habebitis causam intrandi regnum cœleste. Quemadmodum enim unum peccatum trahit ad aliud, sic una actio virtuosa disponit et trahit ad aliam. Et quanto quis diligentius ac frequentius bonis insistit operibus, tanto fit ei facilius et delectabilius talibus immorari.
paras.en: Then another reason is added why we ought to act so. [[1:11|For so an entrance shall be ministered to you abundantly|Sic enim abundanter ministrabitur vobis introitus]], that is, the power of entering will be granted you readily and plentifully by the supreme Judge, [[1:11|into the ever-lasting kingdom of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ|in æternum regnum Domini nostri et Salvatoris Jesu Christi]]: [[Luke 1:33|of his kingdom there shall be no end|cujus regni non erit finis]]. Of which it is written in Daniel: [[Dan 7:14|his power is an everlasting power that shall not be taken away: and his kingdom that shall not be destroyed|Potestas ejus potestas æterna, quæ non auferetur, et regnum ejus quod non corrumpetur]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 144:13|Thy kingdom is a kingdom of all ages|Regnum tuum, regnum omnium sæculorum]] [the margin gives Ps. xliv, 13; the verse is Ps 144:13]. Or: [[1:11|an entrance shall be ministered to you abundantly|Ministrabitur vobis abundanter introitus]] into the kingdom of Christ, because by doing so you will advance daily in all grace and virtue, and will abound in merits, through which you will have the ground for entering the heavenly kingdom. For as one sin draws to another, so one virtuous act disposes and draws to another. And the more diligently and frequently a man applies himself to good works, the easier and more delightful it becomes for him to dwell in them.

paras.t: Propter quod […] monere de his : id est, quia tam fructuosum est et salubre taliter conversari, idcirco indesinenter exhortabor vos ut ita agatis. Quamvis enim beatissimus Petrus corporaliter præsens non fuerit eis quibus hæc scripsit, tamen per hæc sua scripta et per discipulos suos, assidue eos de his adimplendis admonuit. Recteque ait, Incipiam semper, quia quotidie desideravit eos ista perpendere, et quasi de novo cum recenti fervore implere. Ipse quoque affectuosissimus ac ferventissimus Petrus, tam ferventer hæc egit, quasi jugiter in facti hujus principio fuisset. Siquidem principium fervet. Unde in Ecclesiastico legitur : Quum consummaverit homo, tunc incipiet. Propter quod S. Franciscus dicere consuevit : Fratres, incipiamus Deo servire.
paras.en: [[1:12|For which cause|Propter quod]] […] [[1:12|in remembrance of these things|monere de his]] [words are lost here in the print; presumably those of the Vulgate, which reads "I will begin to put you always in remembrance of these things"]: that is, since it is so fruitful and wholesome to live in this way, I will therefore exhort you unceasingly to act so. For although the most blessed Peter was not present in body to those to whom he wrote this, yet by these writings of his and by his disciples he constantly admonished them to fulfil these things. And rightly he says [[1:12|I will begin|Incipiam]] … [[1:12|always|semper]], because he desired them daily to weigh these things, and to fulfil them as if anew, with fresh fervour. And Peter himself, most affectionate and most fervent, did these things so fervently, as if he were ever at the beginning of this work. For a beginning is fervent. Hence we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 18:6|When a man hath done, then shall he begin|Quum consummaverit homo, tunc incipiet]]. For which reason St. Francis used to say: Brothers, let us begin to serve God.

paras.t: Et quidem scientes et confirmatos vos in præsenti veritate : id est, incipiam vos hortari qui estis scientes ea quæ sunt legis divinæ, et estis jam radicati per exercitia diuturna in hac ipsa fidei veritate, quam doceo et tenetis. Sic et Paulus : Scientibus (inquit) legem loquor. Et Joannes in prima sua Canonica : Non scripsi vobis quasi ignorantibus veritatem, sed quasi scientibus eam. — Sed si ista noverunt, et habituati erant in bonis, cur indesinenter voluit eos hortari de istis, nisi ut ea quæ noverunt, factis exsequerentur, et fortius accenderentur, copiosius quoque illuminarentur, actualiter considerando quæ habitualiter cognoscebant, et ne a bonis torperent aut laberentur? Hinc enim in Proverbiis inducitur : Audiens sapiens, sapientior erit. Et rursus Salomon ait : Da sapienti occasionem, et addetur ei sapientia. Si igitur præsidenti molestum non est salubria sæpe repetere, non pigeat subditos ea frequenter audire. Siquidem beati qui audiunt verbum Dei, et custodiunt illud.
paras.en: [[1:12|though indeed you know them and are confirmed in the present truth|Et quidem scientes et confirmatos vos in præsenti veritate]]: that is, I will begin to exhort you, who know the things that belong to the divine law, and are already rooted, by long exercise, in this very truth of the faith which I teach and you hold. So too Paul: [[Rom 7:1|to them that know the law|Scientibus]], he says, [[Rom 7:1|I speak|legem loquor]]. And John in his first Canonical Epistle: [[1 John 2:21|I have not written to you as to them that know not the truth, but as to them that know it|Non scripsi vobis quasi ignorantibus veritatem, sed quasi scientibus eam]]. But if they knew these things, and were practised in good, why did he wish to exhort them unceasingly about them, unless that they might carry out in deeds what they knew, and be more strongly kindled and more abundantly enlightened, by actually considering what they knew habitually [that is, as a settled possession of the mind, not then being thought of], and that they might not grow sluggish in good or fall away from it? For hence it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 1:5|A wise man shall hear, and shall be wiser|Audiens sapiens, sapientior erit]]. And again Solomon says: [[Prov 9:9|Give an occasion to a wise man, and wisdom shall be added to him|Da sapienti occasionem, et addetur ei sapientia]]. If then it is not irksome to the one who presides to repeat wholesome things often, let it not weary his subjects to hear them often. For [[Luke 11:28|blessed are they who hear the word of God and keep it|beati qui audiunt verbum Dei, et custodiunt illud]].

paras.t: Justum autem arbitror, quamdiu sum in hoc tabernaculo, id est, in mortali hoc corpore dego, suscitare vos in commonitione, id est per exhortationem vos provocare ad opera virtuosa. Ad hoc quoque electissimus Petrus ratione pastoralis tenetur officii : et quia Christus præceperat ei, Pasce oves meas ; et alibi, Tu aliquando conversus, confirma fratres tuos. Quod etiam ex fervidissima dilectione strenuissime adimplevit. Nam ut S. Clemens testatur, immensa caritate erat repletus. Unusquisque quoque proximum suum loco et tempore opportuno debet hortari, corripere, informare pro posse, juxta illud Ecclesiastici, Unicuique mandavit Deus de proximo suo : ut utique faciat ei sicut velit sibi fieri.
paras.en: [[1:13|But I think it meet, as long as I am in this tabernacle|Justum autem arbitror, quamdiu sum in hoc tabernaculo]], that is, live in this mortal body, [[1:13|to stir you up by putting you in remembrance|suscitare vos in commonitione]], that is, to rouse you by exhortation to works of virtue. To this the most chosen Peter was bound also by reason of his pastoral office, and because Christ had commanded him: [[John 21:17|Feed my sheep|Pasce oves meas]]; and elsewhere: [[Luke 22:32|thou, being once converted, confirm thy brethren|Tu aliquando conversus, confirma fratres tuos]]. And this he fulfilled most zealously out of a most fervent love. For, as St. Clement testifies, he was filled with boundless charity. Every man, too, ought to exhort, correct and instruct his neighbour as far as he can, at a fitting place and time, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 17:12|he gave to every one of them commandment concerning his neighbour|Unicuique mandavit Deus de proximo suo]]: that is, that he should do to him as he would wish done to himself.

paras.t: Certus quod velox est depositio tabernaculi mei, id est, quod cito recedam a corpore isto, ingressurus regnum cœleste, secundum quod Dominus noster Jesus Christus significavit mihi per revelationem, sive per angelum, sive immediate per se ipsum. Circa hunc locum scribit venerabilis Beda : Tabernaculo solent homines in itinere aut in prælio uti : idcirco fideles, quamdiu sunt in corpore, et peregrinantur a Domino, ac contra veritatis adversarios certant, in tabernaculis se esse rite testantur. Pulcherrime quoque S. Petrus obitum suum non mortem, sed depositionem tabernaculi sui dicit : quoniam sic est perfectis Dei famulis mortalem carnem exuere, sicut viatoribus completo itinere, propriam domum pro tabernaculi habitatione adire, et sicut bellatoribus hoste prostrato, ad patriam regredi, quia non nisi in cœlis reputant sibi esse domum ac patriam.
paras.en: [[1:14|Being assured that the laying away of this my tabernacle is at hand|Certus quod velox est depositio tabernaculi mei]], that is, that I shall soon depart from this body, to enter the heavenly kingdom, [[1:14|according as our Lord Jesus Christ also hath signified to me|secundum quod Dominus noster Jesus Christus significavit mihi]] by revelation [Denis's text adds *per revelationem*, "by revelation", which the Vulgate lacks], whether through an angel or directly by himself. On this place the Venerable Bede writes: Men are wont to use a tent [*tabernaculum*, the Douay's "tabernacle"] on a journey or in battle; therefore the faithful, as long as they are in the body and are absent from the Lord, and fight against the adversaries of the truth, rightly testify that they are in tents. Most beautifully, too, St. Peter calls his passing not death but the laying away of his tabernacle: since for the perfect servants of God to put off the mortal flesh is as for travellers, their journey done, to go to their own home instead of lodging in a tent, and as for warriors, the enemy overthrown, to return to their fatherland; for they reckon that they have no home and fatherland but in heaven.

paras.t: Dabo autem operam, id est, diligentiam efficaciamque impendam, et frequenter vos habere post obitum meum, id est, ut ita vos habeatis post recessum meum a corpore, ut horum memoriam faciatis, id est, ea quæ scribo, doceo ac jubeo, memoriter teneatis, et opere compleatis. Siquidem felicissimus Petrus tam virtuosissime in sua se habuit vita, tam constantissime in passione, tam ferventer in prædicando, tam sapienter in scribendo, tam potenter in miraculis, quæ in vita, in morte, et post martyrii palmam peregit, quod omni memoria et imitatione fuit dignissimus.
paras.en: [[1:15|And I will endeavour|Dabo autem operam]], that is, I will spend care and effort, [[1:15|that you frequently have after my decease|et frequenter vos habere post obitum meum]], that is, that you may so hold yourselves after my departure from the body, [[1:15|whereby you may keep a memory of these things|ut horum memoriam faciatis]]: that is, that you may keep in memory, and fulfil in deed, the things that I write, teach and command. For the most happy Peter bore himself so very virtuously in his life, so very constantly in his passion, so fervently in preaching, so wisely in writing, so powerfully in the miracles which he wrought in life, in death and after the palm of martyrdom, that he was most worthy of all remembrance and imitation.

paras.t: Præterea, sicut in fine expositionis præcedentis epistolæ tactum est, gloriosissimus Petrus primam scripsit epistolam Claudio imperante, antequam S. Marcum evangelistam misit Alexandriam ; hanc vero, ut ipse jam innuit, scripsisse videtur passioni propinquus : sicque longum fuit temporis intervallum inter harum conscriptionem epistolarum.
paras.en: Moreover, as was touched on at the end of the exposition of the preceding epistle[[1 Pet 5:13||]], the most glorious Peter wrote the first epistle in the reign of Claudius, before he sent St. Mark the Evangelist to Alexandria; but this one, as he has just hinted, he seems to have written when near his passion: and so there was a long interval of time between the writing of these epistles.

paras.t: Consequenter tangit Christianæ fidei fundamenta seu argumenta, et quam digna sit ejus doctrina omni memoria. Non enim indoctas, id est falsas et imperitas, fabulas secuti, notam fecimus vobis Domini nostri Jesu Christi virtutem, id est omnipotentiam et deitatem, et præscientiam, id est æternam ejus scientiam, qua invariabiliter ac æternaliter universa intuetur, præterita, præsentia et futura, imo et infinita quæ nec fuerunt, nec sunt, nec erunt. Christus quoque secundum assumptam humanitatem, omnia ab incarnationis exordio novit quæ scit secundum quod Deus, scientia visionis, utpote universa quæ fuerunt, sunt, aut erunt. Hæc autem summus Apostolus notificavit fidelibus, prædicando, miracula faciendo, Scripturas allegando, et ea quæ vidit atque audivit narrando. Pagani autem indoctas poetarum fabulas sequentes, varia deorum portenta finxerunt. Similiter Manichæi et alii quidam hæretici, diversas, inanissimas et mendacissimas fabulas sunt secuti.
paras.en: Next he touches on the foundations or proofs of the Christian faith, and how worthy its teaching is of all remembrance. [[1:16|For we have not by following artificial|Non enim indoctas]], that is, false and unskilled, [[1:16|fables|fabulas secuti]] [Denis reads *indoctas*, "unlearned", where the Vulgate has *doctas*, "learned", that is, cunningly devised; hence his gloss], [[1:16|made known to you the power|notam fecimus vobis Domini nostri Jesu Christi virtutem]], that is, his almightiness and godhead, [[1:16|and presence of our Lord Jesus Christ|et præscientiam]] [Denis reads *præscientiam*, "foreknowledge", where the Vulgate has *præsentiam*, "presence"], that is, his eternal knowledge, by which he beholds all things unchangeably and eternally, past, present and future, nay, even the infinite things that neither have been, nor are, nor will be. Christ too, according to the humanity he assumed, knew from the beginning of the incarnation all that he knows as God by the knowledge of vision [that is, God's knowledge of all that is real at any time, as distinct from his knowledge of what is merely possible], namely all things that have been, are, or will be. These things the chief Apostle made known to the faithful by preaching, by working miracles, by bringing forward the Scriptures, and by telling what he had seen and heard. But the pagans, following the unlearned fables of the poets, invented various monstrous tales of gods. In like manner the Manichees and certain other heretics followed diverse, most empty and most lying fables.

paras.t: Sed speculatores facti illius magnitudinis, id est, nos effecti contemplatores majestatis et excellentiæ Christi, notificamus virtutem et præscientiam ejus. Unde in Joanne habetur : Vidimus gloriam ejus, gloriam quasi Unigeniti a Patre. Viderunt sancti Apostoli oculo corporali Christi humanitatem atque miracula ; interiorique oculo per fidem illuminatam et sapientiæ donum, conspexerunt ejus divinæ excellentiam majestatis. Similiter post resurrectionem viderunt eminentiam Christi in multis : quomodo januis clausis ad eos ingressus est, et Spiritum Sanctum per insufflationem contulit eis. Ipsis quoque videntibus ascendit in cœlum, deinde in signo visibili, et abundantissima gratiæ copia misit eis Spiritum Sanctum. Hinc in Actibus præstantissimus loquitur Petrus : Non possumus ea quæ audivimus et vidimus, non loqui.
paras.en: [[1:16|but we were eyewitnesses of his greatness|Sed speculatores facti illius magnitudinis]], that is, having been made beholders of the majesty and excellence of Christ, we make known his power and foreknowledge. Hence it is said in John: [[John 1:14|we saw his glory, the glory as it were of the only begotten of the Father|Vidimus gloriam ejus, gloriam quasi Unigeniti a Patre]]. The holy Apostles saw with the bodily eye the humanity and the miracles of Christ; and with the inner eye, through enlightened faith and the gift of wisdom, they beheld the excellence of his divine majesty. Likewise after the resurrection they saw the eminence of Christ in many things: how he came in to them, [[John 20:26|the doors being shut|januis clausis]], and conferred the Holy Ghost on them by breathing on them[[John 20:22||]] [the margin gives John xx, 26, 27; the breathing is at John 20:22]. Also, while they looked on, he ascended into heaven[[Acts 1:9||]]; and then he sent them the Holy Ghost under a visible sign and with a most abundant plenty of grace[[Acts 2:1||]]. Hence the most excellent Peter says in the Acts: [[Acts 4:20|we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard|Non possumus ea quæ audivimus et vidimus, non loqui]].

paras.t: Accepit enim a Patre honorem et gloriam, id est honorificam et gloriosam attestationem, seu testimonium honorabilitatis et gloriæ, voce delapsa, id est desuper veniente, ad eum a magnifica gloria, id est a magnificentia et excellentia Dei Patris.
paras.en: [[1:17|For he received from God the Father honour and glory|Accepit enim a Patre honorem et gloriam]], that is, an honourable and glorious attestation, or testimony of honour and glory, [[1:17|this voice coming down|voce delapsa]], that is, coming from above, [[1:17|to him from the excellent glory|ad eum a magnifica gloria]], that is, from the magnificence and excellence of God the Father.

paras.t: Et quæ fuerit illa vox, id est complexio vocum, subjungitur : Hic est Filius meus dilectus, id est naturalis et unicus, consubstantialis, coæqualis, coæternus, non adoptivus : quem, secundum quod Deus est, diligo non minus quam me ipsum, utpote dilectione intensiva, immensa, quum infinitæ sit bonitatis, et mihi vere æqualis. Porro, in quantum est homo, prout ejus humanitas unita est hypostatica unione Verbo æterno, diligo eum magis quam totum universum. Sic enim Pater contulit Christi humanitati, in eodem esse personali subsistere in quo consistit Verbum æternum : quod subsistere, reliquum omne bonum creatum excedit.
paras.en: And what that voice was, that is, that combination of words, is added[[Matt 17:5||]]: [[1:17|This is my beloved Son|Hic est Filius meus dilectus]], that is, natural and only, consubstantial, coequal, coeternal, not adopted; whom, as he is God, I love not less than myself, namely with an intensive, boundless love, since he is of infinite goodness and truly equal to me. Further, in so far as he is man, inasmuch as his humanity is united to the eternal Word by the hypostatic union, I love him more than the whole universe. For thus the Father granted to the humanity of Christ to subsist in the same personal being in which the eternal Word subsists: and this subsisting surpasses all other created good.

paras.t: In quo mihi complacui, id est, beneplacitum fuit mihi. Si enim beneplacitum est Domino in populo suo, et lætatur Dominus in operibus suis : quanto magis in unigenito Filio suo, in quo utique Pater habet complacentiam penitus infinitam? In se ipso quoque Pater complacentiam habet prorsus immensam. Et complacet sibi in Filio suo, id est, de hoc Pater sibi ipsi complacet infinite, quod talem ac tantum genuit Filium, et quod in se ipso tantæ bonitatis ac fecunditatis consistit, ut consubstantialem sibi peperit natum, sibi omnino simillimum, in nullo a se discordem, quum ejusdem secum sit voluntatis, quemadmodum et unius essentiæ.
paras.en: [[1:17|in whom I am well pleased|In quo mihi complacui]], that is, it was my good pleasure. For if [[Ps 149:4|the Lord is well pleased with his people|beneplacitum est Domino in populo suo]], and [[Ps 103:31|the Lord shall rejoice in his works|lætatur Dominus in operibus suis]], how much more in his only-begotten Son, in whom indeed the Father has a wholly infinite complacency [that is, delight and good pleasure]? In himself too the Father has an altogether boundless complacency. And he is well pleased with himself in his Son: that is, the Father is infinitely pleased with himself in this, that he has begotten such and so great a Son, and that he is in himself of such goodness and fruitfulness that he has brought forth a Son consubstantial with himself, altogether most like himself, in nothing at variance with him, since he is of the same will with him, as also of one essence.

paras.t: Fertur autem hæc vox ministerio prolata angelico, in Dei Patris persona. Ipsum audite auribus cordis et corporis, et credite obediteque ei. Unde ipse Christus testatur : Omnis qui est ex veritate, audit vocem meam.
paras.en: Now this voice is said to have been uttered by the ministry of an angel, in the person of God the Father. [[1:17|Hear ye him|Ipsum audite]] with the ears of the heart and of the body, and believe and obey him. Hence Christ himself testifies: [[John 18:37|Every one that is of the truth heareth my voice|Omnis qui est ex veritate, audit vocem meam]].

paras.t: Et hanc vocem nos audivimus de cœlo allatam, id est cœlesti virtute formatam, atque in cœlo aerio factam, quum essemus cum ipso in monte sancto. Hæc enim vox facta est in Christi transfiguratione in monte Thabor, qui propter transfigurationem Christi in eo peractam, vocatur mons sanctus. Cui transfigurationi interfuerunt Apostoli præclari, Petrus, Jacobus et Joannes filii Zebedæi. De qua transfiguratione et apparitione, super Matthæum et Lucam diffusius scripsi : idcirco nunc transeo.
paras.en: [[1:18|And this voice, we heard brought from heaven|Et hanc vocem nos audivimus de cœlo allatam]], that is, formed by heavenly power, and made in the heaven of the air [that is, in the sky, not in the heaven of the blessed], [[1:18|when we were with him in the holy mount|quum essemus cum ipso in monte sancto]]. For this voice came at the transfiguration of Christ on Mount Thabor, which is called the holy mount because of the transfiguration of Christ accomplished on it. At this transfiguration the illustrious Apostles were present, Peter, and James and John the sons of Zebedee. Of this transfiguration and apparition I have written more fully on Matthew and Luke[[Matt 17:1||]][[Luke 9:28||]]: therefore I now pass over it.

paras.t: Consequenter Christi divinitatem probat testimonio prophetali irrefragabili. Et habemus firmiorem, id est valde firmum, propheticum sermonem, id est testimonium David regis de Christi divinitate in psalmo ubi loquitur Filius : Dominus dixit ad me : Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Imo in pluribus psalmis loquitur David inde : ut est illud, Ex utero ante luciferum genui te ; et, Eructavit cor meum verbum bonum.
